newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians register to vote under tightened rules.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians register to vote under tightened rules.

text.p: Bosnian voters began registering on Monday for municipal elections which have three times been postponed due to abuses.
International supervisors said they had drawn up measures to prevent irregularities in the polls, now scheduled for September.
More than 400 centres opened across Bosnia for a six-week registration period supervised by monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
The OSCE mission had postponed the local polls three times due to widespread irregularities reported in the registration of refugees.
The municipal vote will decide the political fate of towns which were fought over by rival armies during more than three years of war which accompanied old Yugoslavia's disintegration.
Serb and other authorities were accused last year of trying to stack the electoral odds in their favour by forcing refugees to register in hotly-contested municipalities.
Rules for this year's vote, designed to prevent "ethnic engineering" by nationalist authorities, set registration criteria for refugees living outside the country.
Refugees abroad can register in municipalities where they "intend" to live, but must prove with documents that they have property or other legal ties to a town.
Under the OSCE rules, voters living in Bosnia can register in their pre-war municipalities or in towns where they have resettled.
OSCE officials said that the registration drive would create a voters' list for future polls and help prevent allegations of voter fraud which plagued general elections held last year.

"During the September 1996 elections we encountered certain administrative difficulties and after the elections were over we decided to draw some lessons from the experience," Robert Frowick, head of the OSCE mission, told a news conference.
The OSCE had no comprehensive voters' list in last year's elections, no reliable list of those killed during the Bosnian war and too few observers to monitor hundreds of polling stations.
"The degree of supervision which we had last year was probably short of what was needed," Frowick said.
The OSCE planned to increase the number of election observers for the municipal vote and expected to have 2,300 supervisors or at least one for every polling station, officials said.
September's general elections -- the first since fighting ended in 1995 -- created a peacetime government for Bosnia, which is divided into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
But the inter-ethnic government has been virtually paralysed, with rival Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders unable to reach agreement on major issues.
